title: DGFiP reports that Foncier innovant detected 140,000 taxable pools in 2023, with a different overview giving more than 120,000
summary: DGFiP’s 2023 annual report attributes 140,000 taxable pool detections and €40 million in added local revenue to Foncier innovant. Another section gives more than 120,000 pools.
account: On 20 March 2024 Thomas Cazenave, minister for public accounts, presented the first bilan of the government's anti-fraud plan at Bercy. He said the DGFiP's algorithmic tool, Foncier innovant, introduced in October 2021, had detected 140,000 undeclared swimming pools. The tool detects pools and buildings on IGN aerial photographs and compares them with declarations. An agent then checks each detection. That would let local authorities collect about €40 million in property tax. Owners received DGFiP letters asking them to regularize (RMC, Ouest-France, L'Indépendant, 21 March 2024). CNews (11 June 2024) cites the DGFiP annual activity report as reported by Ouest-France. It gives 140,000 pools identified in 2023 and €40 million that should have been paid in 2023. That compares with 20,000 pools in the 2022 experiment in nine départements (20 Minutes). L'Indépendant instead states 120,000 for 2022, so the press accounts of the yearly split disagree. At département level, ici (France Bleu) reported on 24 March 2024 on the Dordogne public-finance office. It had found about 1,500 undeclared pools in 2023 among some 30,000 in the département. It would send property-tax catch-up notices by the end of March. DGFiP’s original 2023 annual report is now available. Its pool-control section reports 140,000 taxable pools in 2023, compared with 20,000 in 2022, and €40 million in additional local property-tax revenue. Its separate cadastral overview says more than 120,000 pools, an internal numerical difference that remains unresolved. No commune-level result was found.
purpose: Detect undeclared pools and buildings from aerial imagery so that they are added to the cadastral base and taxed. This was the tool's intended purpose.
system: Foncier innovant (DGFiP deep-learning detection of pools and buildings on IGN aerial photographs, built with Capgemini and Google)

fields.account: On 20 March 2024 Thomas Cazenave, minister for public accounts, presented the first bilan of the government's anti-fraud plan at Bercy. He said the DGFiP's algorithmic tool, Foncier innovant, introduced in October 2021, had detected 140,000 undeclared swimming pools. The tool detects pools and buildings on IGN aerial photographs and compares them with declarations. An agent then checks each detection. That would let local authorities collect about €40 million in property tax. Owners received DGFiP letters asking them to regularize (RMC, Ouest-France, L'Indépendant, 21 March 2024). CNews (11 June 2024) cites the DGFiP annual activity report as reported by Ouest-France. It gives 140,000 pools identified in 2023 and €40 million that should have been paid in 2023. That compares with 20,000 pools in the 2022 experiment in nine départements (20 Minutes). L'Indépendant instead states 120,000 for 2022, so the press accounts of the yearly split disagree. At département level, ici (France Bleu) reported on 24 March 2024 on the Dordogne public-finance office. It had found about 1,500 undeclared pools in 2023 among some 30,000 in the département. It would send property-tax catch-up notices by the end of March. DGFiP’s original 2023 annual report is now available. Its pool-control section reports 140,000 taxable pools in 2023, compared with 20,000 in 2022, and €40 million in additional local property-tax revenue. Its separate cadastral overview says more than 120,000 pools, an internal numerical difference that remains unresolved. No commune-level result was found.

fields.summary: DGFiP’s 2023 annual report attributes 140,000 taxable pool detections and €40 million in added local revenue to Foncier innovant. Another section gives more than 120,000 pools.
fields.account: On 20 March 2024 Thomas Cazenave, minister for public accounts, presented the first bilan of the government's anti-fraud plan at Bercy. He said the DGFiP's algorithmic tool, Foncier innovant, introduced in October 2021, had detected 140,000 undeclared swimming pools. The tool detects pools and buildings on IGN aerial photographs and compares them with declarations. An agent then checks each detection. That would let local authorities collect about €40 million in property tax. Owners received DGFiP letters asking them to regularize (RMC, Ouest-France, L'Indépendant, 21 March 2024). CNews (11 June 2024) cites the DGFiP annual activity report as reported by Ouest-France. It gives 140,000 pools identified in 2023 and €40 million that should have been paid in 2023. That compares with 20,000 pools in the 2022 experiment in nine départements (20 Minutes). L'Indépendant instead states 120,000 for 2022, so the press accounts of the yearly split disagree. At département level, ici (France Bleu) reported on 24 March 2024 on the Dordogne public-finance office. It had found about 1,500 undeclared pools in 2023 among some 30,000 in the département. It would send property-tax catch-up notices by the end of March. DGFiP’s original 2023 annual report is now available. Its pool-control section reports 140,000 taxable pools in 2023, compared with 20,000 in 2022, and €40 million in additional local property-tax revenue. Its separate cadastral overview says more than 120,000 pools, an internal numerical difference that remains unresolved. No commune-level result was found.
